questiontext.text:
Triangle \(ABC\) (green) and triangle \(A'B'C'\) (blue) are shown on the grid. The point \(O\) marks a fixed centre.

Drag the slider to rotate the dashed copy of triangle \(ABC\) about \(O\). Use it to investigate whether triangle \(ABC\) can be turned exactly onto triangle \(A'B'C'\).

[[jsxgraph width="560px" height="560px"]] var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, { boundingbox: [-10, 10, 10, -10], axis: true, showCopyright: false, showNavigation: false, keepaspectratio: true, grid: true }); /* ---- Original triangle ABC (fixed) ---- */ var A = board.create('point', [{#Ax#}, {#Ay#}], {name:'A', size:3, color:'#2e7d32', fixed:true, label:{offset:[6,6]}}); var B = board.create('point', [{#Bx#}, {#By#}], {name:'B', size:3, color:'#2e7d32', fixed:true, label:{offset:[6,6]}}); var C = board.create('point', [{#Cx#}, {#Cy#}], {name:'C', size:3, color:'#2e7d32', fixed:true, label:{offset:[6,6]}}); board.create('polygon', [A, B, C], { fillColor:'#a5d6a7', fillOpacity:0.55, borders:{strokeColor:'#2e7d32', strokeWidth:2}, vertices:{visible:false} }); /* ---- Image triangle A'B'C' (fixed) ---- */ var Ap = board.create('point', [{#Sx#}, {#Sy#}], {name:"A'", size:3, color:'#1565c0', fixed:true, label:{offset:[6,6]}}); var Bp = board.create('point', [{#Tx#}, {#Ty#}], {name:"B'", size:3, color:'#1565c0', fixed:true, label:{offset:[6,6]}}); var Cp = board.create('point', [{#Vx#}, {#Vy#}], {name:"C'", size:3, color:'#1565c0', fixed:true, label:{offset:[6,6]}}); board.create('polygon', [Ap, Bp, Cp], { fillColor:'#90caf9', fillOpacity:0.55, borders:{strokeColor:'#1565c0', strokeWidth:2}, vertices:{visible:false} }); /* ---- Centre of rotation O (bright, unmistakable) ---- */ var O = board.create('point', [{#Ox#}, {#Oy#}], { name:'O', size:5, color:'#d500f9', fixed:true, face:'o', strokeColor:'#000000', strokeWidth:1, fillColor:'#d500f9', label:{offset:[10,-6], fontSize:16, cssStyle:'font-weight:bold'} }); /* ---- Angle slider (0 to 360 degrees), placed clearly inside the top of the board ---- */ var sl = board.create('slider', [[-9, 9], [-1, 9], [0, 0, 360]], { name:'θ', snapWidth:15, precision:0, fillColor:'#e65100', strokeColor:'#e65100', size:5, label:{offset:[6,10], fontSize:15, cssStyle:'font-weight:bold'} }); /* rotate point (px,py) about O by the slider angle (anticlockwise, degrees) */ var gA = board.create('point', [function(){ var t = sl.Value()*Math.PI/180, ox=O.X(), oy=O.Y(), dx={#Ax#}-ox, dy={#Ay#}-oy; return ox + dx*Math.cos(t) - dy*Math.sin(t); }, function(){ var t = sl.Value()*Math.PI/180, ox=O.X(), oy=O.Y(), dx={#Ax#}-ox, dy={#Ay#}-oy; return oy + dx*Math.sin(t) + dy*Math.cos(t); }], {visible:false, name:''}); var gB = board.create('point', [function(){ var t = sl.Value()*Math.PI/180, ox=O.X(), oy=O.Y(), dx={#Bx#}-ox, dy={#By#}-oy; return ox + dx*Math.cos(t) - dy*Math.sin(t); }, function(){ var t = sl.Value()*Math.PI/180, ox=O.X(), oy=O.Y(), dx={#Bx#}-ox, dy={#By#}-oy; return oy + dx*Math.sin(t) + dy*Math.cos(t); }], {visible:false, name:''}); var gC = board.create('point', [function(){ var t = sl.Value()*Math.PI/180, ox=O.X(), oy=O.Y(), dx={#Cx#}-ox, dy={#Cy#}-oy; return ox + dx*Math.cos(t) - dy*Math.sin(t); }, function(){ var t = sl.Value()*Math.PI/180, ox=O.X(), oy=O.Y(), dx={#Cx#}-ox, dy={#Cy#}-oy; return oy + dx*Math.sin(t) + dy*Math.cos(t); }], {visible:false, name:''}); /* dashed "ghost" copy that the student turns with the slider */ board.create('polygon', [gA, gB, gC], { fillColor:'#ff9800', fillOpacity:0.20, borders:{strokeColor:'#e65100', strokeWidth:2, dash:2}, vertices:{visible:false} }); /* faint radius from O to a ghost vertex, to make the turning visible */ board.create('segment', [O, gA], {strokeColor:'#e65100', strokeWidth:1, dash:1}); [[/jsxgraph]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

Two figures are congruent when one can be mapped exactly onto the other by a rigid transformation (an isometry): a translation, rotation, reflection, or a combination of these. Rigid transformations preserve every side length and every angle, so the shape and size are unchanged.

A rotation turns a figure about a fixed centre through a given angle. It preserves distances (so figures stay congruent) and also preserves orientation — the vertices keep the same cyclic order (here \(A\to A',\ B\to B',\ C\to C'\)).

This variant:

{@sol_text@}

How to find the centre and angle of a rotation:

  • Join each point to its image: \(A\to A'\), \(B\to B'\), \(C\to C'\).
  • Construct the perpendicular bisector of each segment. All the perpendicular bisectors meet at a single point — that point is the centre of rotation \(O\).
  • The angle of rotation is the angle \(A\,\hat{O}\,A'\), measured anticlockwise.

In the interactive figure you can confirm this: set the slider to the angle and the dashed copy of \(ABC\) lands exactly on \(A'B'C'\) when the rotation is correct.

questiondescription.text:
Sheila Cherotich

Congruence and rotation as a rigid transformation; finding centre and angle of rotation.

The learner uses an interactive slider to rotate a copy of a triangle about a marked centre, decides whether the two triangles are congruent, names the transformation, and (for rotations) states the centre and angle. Some variants are deliberately not congruent (a non-isometric vertical stretch) so the learner must reason from side lengths rather than assume congruence.

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

falsefeedback.text: Compare the side lengths of the two triangles. Congruent figures must have exactly the same side lengths and angles. Use the slider to test whether \(ABC\) can be turned onto \(A'B'C'\).

The vertices keep the same order \(A\to A',\ B\to B',\ C\to C'\) (orientation is preserved) and every point moves along a circular arc about a fixed centre. Which single transformation does that — or are the figures not congruent at all?

The centre of rotation is the one point that stays fixed. Find it as the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of \(AA'\), \(BB'\) and \(CC'\), or use the slider: the correct centre is the marked point \(O\) about which the dashed copy turns onto \(A'B'C'\).
Measure the turn from \(A\) to \(A'\) about \(O\), anticlockwise. Setting the slider to the angle of rotation lands the dashed triangle exactly on \(A'B'C'\).
These two figures are not congruent, so no rotation maps one onto the other. The angle of rotation is "Not applicable" here.

qtest.description: All four parts correct earns full marks (works for both rotation and not-congruent variants).
Congruence question answered wrongly loses part (a).
